chapterTitle: Collaborative Development with GitHub & Branching Strategies
aiGenerationNote:
Generate a 10-14 minute interactive lab walkthrough focusing on Git branching and GitHub Pull Requests. The video should start by visually explaining the concept of a branch as a separate timeline. Then, perform a live coding demonstration:
1.  Creating a new branch (`git checkout -b feature/new-feature`).
2.  Making changes and committing them on the feature branch.
3.  Switching back to `main` and making a conflicting change.
4.  Attempting to merge the feature branch into `main`, showing the merge conflict markers clearly in an IDE (e.g., VS Code or IntelliJ).
5.  Step-by-step resolution of the conflict, demonstrating how to edit the file and remove markers.
6.  Staging and committing the resolved merge.
7.  Briefly show the GitHub interface for creating a Pull Request from the feature branch to `main`, highlighting the code review aspect.
The tone should be hands-on and problem-solving, emphasizing that merge conflicts are normal and resolvable. Use clear visual indicators for current branch and file status. Include an interactive element where learners are prompted to identify the conflicting sections in a provided code snippet.

screens.title: Collaborative Development with GitHub & Branching Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how teams coordinate work using remote repositories and branching. You will learn how platforms like GitHub host your repository online so teammates can push, pull, review, and merge code. More than file storage, GitHub gives you Issues, Pull Requests, and a visible history that supports collaboration and review for quality. We’ll also unpack branching: why you create isolated branches for features or fixes, how to switch and commit on those branches, and how merging brings changes back into a stable main branch. You will see a concrete scenario where a feature branch and main both change the same file, produce a merge conflict, and how to resolve it safely. Finally, we’ll compare simple GitHub Flow and the more structured Git Flow so you can choose a branching strategy that fits your project. By the end, you’ll understand the social and technical steps—create branch, commit, push, open a Pull Request, review, merge—so your team can evolve code confidently. Consider how this workflow preserves a deployable main branch while enabling many parallel contributors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you will build practical skills for collaborative Git workflows. First, you will explain the role of GitHub and similar hosting platforms: what happens when you push or pull, and why a remote repository matters for team visibility. Second, you will understand branching as an isolated line of development and when to choose a new branch for a feature or a hotfix. Third, you will create, switch between, and merge branches using real commands, and practice committing and pushing your changes so others can review them. Fourth, you will identify and resolve merge conflicts that occur when two branches change the same lines, and demonstrate the correct staging and commit steps to finalize a merge. Each objective emphasizes both the commands and the reasoning behind them, so you can apply the workflow on your team. We'll use concrete examples like adding a Calculator class and simulating conflicting edits to HelloWorld. java to practice these skills. By the end, you'll confidently open a Pull Request, respond to review feedback, and integrate changes while keeping main deployable.

screens.title: Practical Skills Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on applied practice. You will learn the precise sequence of commands used in a typical feature workflow: create a branch, make commits, push the branch to the remote, open a Pull Request, handle requested changes, and merge. We reinforce the correct conflict workflow: when Git stops a merge, inspect the conflict markers, edit to decide what to keep, stage the resolved files with git add, then commit to finish the merge. You will practice both the safe habit of keeping main deployable and the practical habit of pulling main into long-lived feature branches frequently to reduce conflict complexity. Practical Skills Checklist
Memorize these sequences and practice them during the lab walkthrough.
Create & Switch
git checkout -b feature/add-calculator or git switch -c feature/add-calculator. Commit changes on the branch and push to origin.
Merge & Conflicts
Switch to main, git merge feature branch. If conflicts appear, edit markers, git add resolved files, then git commit to complete the merge.
Pull Request Flow
Push feature branch, open a Pull Request targeting main, request reviews, address feedback, and merge when approved.
Quick Command Reference
git checkout -b feature/add-calculator
git switch feature/add-calculator
git add Calculator.java
git commit -m "feat: Added Calculator class"
git switch main
git merge feature/add-calculator
# resolve conflicts if any
git add HelloWorld.java
git commit -m "Merge feature/add-calculator into main"

screens.title: What is a Remote Repository and Why GitHub?
screens.narratorSegment: A remote repository is the shared copy of your project that lives on a hosting service such as GitHub. The remote stores commits pushed by contributors and acts as the authoritative source for collaboration. When you run git push, your local commits are uploaded to the remote so teammates can fetch or pull them into their local clones. Conversely, git pull fetches and merges remote commits into your current branch. GitHub adds social and workflow tools on top of this: Issues to track bugs and requests, Pull Requests for proposing code integration, and a web-based diff viewer for reviews. This combination is powerful: it separates local experimentation from shared history and creates a visible record that supports review, discussion, and CI automation. For a concrete example, if one teammate pushes a feature branch called feature/add-calculator, others can open that branch on GitHub, comment on specific lines, and run tests against it before merging. A common misconception is thinking the remote replaces local history; instead, it complements local repositories by providing a central place to coordinate and recover work. Key takeaway: push and pull are the networked actions that connect local branches to the team’s shared workflow, enabling review and integration without forcing everyone to share a single working copy.

keyIdea.title: Remote role
keyIdea.text: GitHub stores shared history, exposes branches for review, and supports Pull Requests and issues that turn commits into collaborative work.

content.html:
Core Concept
Remote Repository & GitHub
GitHub hosts a remote copy of your repo and layers collaboration tools like Issues and Pull Requests on top.
Push and Pull: share and receive commits with git push and git pull.
Visibility: branches pushed to the remote are visible for review and CI.
Review: Pull Requests let teammates discuss changes before merging.
Key Takeaway

A remote is the team’s shared timeline. GitHub adds review, issues, and integration so collaboration scales safely.

Concrete Example
A developer creates feature/add-calculator locally, commits changes, then runs:
git push origin feature/add-calculator
Now teammates can open a Pull Request on GitHub that shows the diff, run tests, and comment on lines. This preserves the main branch until the code is approved and merged.
Common Misconception
Some learners think pushing immediately makes code live in production. In reality, pushing shares commits to the remote; deployment depends on your CI/CD and merge policies.

screens.title: Branching: an Independent Line of Development
screens.narratorSegment: Branching creates an independent line of development that lets you work on a feature or fix without affecting the stable main branch. Conceptually, each branch is a pointer into the commit history; commits made on that branch form a separate timeline. Choose branch names that communicate purpose, for example feature/add-calculator or fix/typo-hello. Good names make code review and repository navigation easier for teammates. The default branch is usually main. When you initialize a repository, you start on main and then create short-lived branches for work. This isolation is crucial: if your feature fails tests or introduces bugs, main remains deployable. A common mistake is doing large, long-lived work on a branch without regularly syncing with main. That increases the chance of complex conflicts later. Instead, keep branches small and integrate often. For a concrete example, create feature/add-calculator and implement Calculator. java with an add method, commit, and push. This keeps the new code separate until reviewers approve it. Takeaway: branch early, commit often, and favor short-lived feature branches so integration is predictable and reviewable. Branching: an Independent Line of Development means branches let teams develop in parallel without destabilizing the main codebase; small, descriptive branches make review and merging easier.. In practical terms, why branches isolate work and how to pick a branch name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Branching
A branch is an independent pointer into commit history. Use branches to isolate features or fixes.
Naming: feature/..., fix/..., hotfix/... — be descriptive and consistent.
Best practice: make branches short-lived and integrate often to reduce conflicts.
Common mistake: very long-lived branches that drift far from main and complicate merges.
Example command: git checkout -b feature/add-calculator creates and switches to the new branch in one step.
Concrete Example: Calculator
// MyJavaProject/Calculator.java
public class Calculator {
  public int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
  }
}
Implementing this class on a feature branch keeps main untouched until the feature is reviewed and merged.
Key Takeaway

Branches are your sandbox. Use descriptive names and merge early to avoid painful conflicts.

screens.title: Create, Switch, and Commit on Branches
screens.narratorSegment: Practically creating and switching branches is how you start isolated work. The commands are straightforward: git branch creates a branch, git switch or git checkout changes your working branch, and git checkout -b or git switch -c creates and switches in a single step. In this walkthrough you’ll enact a realistic sequence: start on main, create feature/add-calculator, add Calculator. java, stage and commit, then push the branch to the remote. The example code for Calculator. java is a minimal class with an add method. Commit messages should be clear and conventional, for example feat: Added Calculator class with add method. A common misconception is that commits made on a branch affect main immediately — they do not until you merge. Another pitfall is forgetting to push your branch; your teammates cannot review or open a Pull Request without the branch on the remote. Practice these commands until they are routine. After committing locally, push with git push origin feature/add-calculator. This sequence prepares the branch for review and eventual integration. Closing question: when would you prefer git switch -c over separate branch and switch commands?

keyIdea.title: Command sequence
keyIdea.text: Create and switch with git switch or git checkout -b, commit your changes, and push the branch so others can review it.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create, Switch, Commit
Follow these commands in sequence to prepare a feature branch for review.
git switch main
git switch -c feature/add-calculator
# create Calculator.java
git add Calculator.java
git commit -m "feat: Added Calculator class with add method"
# push branch for remote review
git push origin feature/add-calculator
Pro tip: keep commit messages short and descriptive. A clear message helps reviewers and future history searches.
Editor View: Calculator.java
// MyJavaProject/Calculator.java
public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
Common Misconception
Committing on a branch does not change main. Only after merging does main include those commits. Keep that boundary in mind when testing locally.

screens.title: Merging Branches: Fast-Forward and Three-Way
screens.narratorSegment: Merging brings changes from one branch into another. There are two common merge outcomes. If the target branch has no new commits since the feature branched, Git can perform a fast-forward merge by simply moving the target pointer forward to include the feature commits. This produces a linear history and is common for short-lived feature branches. The other outcome uses a three-way merge: when both branches have diverged, Git creates a merge commit that combines the histories. Three-way merges can introduce merge conflicts when the same lines in a file were changed differently. To merge, switch to the target branch, for example git switch main, then run git merge feature/add-calculator. If the merge is automatic, you’re done. If a conflict appears, Git pauses. A common misconception is thinking a merge always rewrites history; it does not unless you use rebase. Merging preserves history and records the branch integration point. Concrete example: after developing Calculator on a feature branch and updating HelloWorld on main, merging will produce either a fast-forward or a merge commit depending on main’s changes. Key takeaway: understand which merge type you expect and keep branches current to reduce surprises.

keyIdea.title: Merge types
keyIdea.text: Fast-forward moves the branch pointer; three-way creates a merge commit. Conflicts happen when both branches change the same lines.

content.html:
Process Flow
Merging Branches
Switch to the target branch and run git merge. Git decides whether to fast-forward or create a merge commit.
Fast-forward: target has no new commits; branch pointer moves forward.
Three-way merge: histories diverged; Git creates a merge commit combining work.
Conflicts: occur when both branches edited the same lines; manual resolution required.
Key Takeaway

Merging preserves history. Keep branches updated to minimize complex three-way merges and conflicts.

Command Example
git switch main
git merge feature/add-calculator
If Git reports merge conflict, it will list affected files and leave conflict markers in those files for you to edit.
Misconception
Rebasing can produce cleaner history but rewrites commits. Merging preserves the true historical record of parallel work.

screens.title: Understanding Merge Conflicts and Markers
screens.narratorSegment: A merge conflict happens when Git cannot reconcile two changes to the same part of a file. Git annotates the file with three markers: the section from your current branch begins after >>>>>> branch-name. Your task is to open the file, review both versions, decide which lines to keep or how to combine them, and then remove all markers. After editing, you must stage the resolved file with git add and then commit to finish the merge. A common mistake is to resolve the textual conflict but forget to git add the file; Git will continue to wait for the staged resolution and you cannot complete the merge. Another pitfall is to accept one side blindly when a combined or reconciled version is better. Use your editor or IDE merge tools where possible, and run your tests after resolving. For a concrete walkthrough, we’ll use HelloWorld. java, which gets different console lines on main and on the feature branch. Resolve by keeping both lines or choosing the best phrasing, then stage and commit. The closing insight: conflicts are normal—treat them as a deliberate code-review moment and communicate with your teammate if unsure.

keyIdea.title: Conflict markers
keyIdea.text: Edit between markers, remove them, stage the resolved files, then commit. Never forget to git add after resolving conflicts.

content.html:
Definition
Merge Conflicts
When both branches edit the same lines, Git asks you to reconcile the differences manually.
Markers: <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>> feature-branch show the conflicting sections.
Resolution steps: edit file, remove markers, git add, git commit.
Common mistake: editing but not staging the resolved file before committing.
Conflict Example: HelloWorld.java
// MyJavaProject/HelloWorld.java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Git!");
        System.out.println("This is my first Git-tracked change.");
<<<<<<< HEAD
        System.out.println("Main branch update.");
=======
        System.out.println("Feature branch update!");
>>>>>>> feature/add-calculator
    }
}
Resolve by choosing one line, or keep both. After editing, run git add HelloWorld.java and git commit -m "Merge feature/add-calculator into main" to finish.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Create a Branch and Simulate a Conflict
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on walkthrough we simulate the full scenario from the chapter. Start on main and create a feature branch with git checkout -b feature/add-calculator. Add Calculator. java, stage, and commit. Then switch back to main and modify HelloWorld. java to add a line that will conflict. Commit that change on main. Switch back to the feature branch, and modify the same section of HelloWorld. java with a different line, then commit. Now switch to main and attempt git merge feature/add-calculator. Git will detect the conflicting edits and stop the merge with conflict markers in HelloWorld. java. You will see markers showing the main branch content and the incoming feature branch content. Your task is to open the file, decide whether to keep one line or both, remove the markers, add the file to staging, and commit. This practice solidifies the flow of create, commit, switch, and merge, revealing how conflicts manifest in real code. A common misconception is that merges always succeed; in practice, frequent merges and small branches reduce conflict complexity. Final question: after resolving, should you delete the feature branch? Yes, when it’s merged and no longer needed, delete to keep the remote tidy.

keyIdea.title: Simulate & resolve
keyIdea.text: Reproduce the conflict by making divergent edits, then resolve markers, stage, and commit to finalize the merge.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Commands to run
# On main
git switch main
# Create feature branch
git checkout -b feature/add-calculator
# Add Calculator and commit
# ... edit files ...
git add Calculator.java
git commit -m "feat: Added Calculator class with add method"
# Simulate conflicting change on main
git switch main
# edit HelloWorld.java and commit
git add HelloWorld.java
git commit -m "refactor: Updated HelloWorld on main branch"
# Edit HelloWorld differently on feature branch
git switch feature/add-calculator
# edit HelloWorld.java and commit
git add HelloWorld.java
git commit -m "feat: Updated HelloWorld on feature branch"
# Attempt merge
git switch main
git merge feature/add-calculator
Expected Result
Git reports a conflict and leaves HelloWorld.java with markers. Open the file, resolve the conflict, then run:
git add HelloWorld.java
git commit -m "Merge feature/add-calculator into main, resolved conflict in HelloWorld.java"
# Optionally delete branch
git branch -d feature/add-calculator
git push origin --delete feature/add-calculator
Run your tests after merging to confirm the combined change behaves as expected.

screens.title: Pull Requests: Social and Technical Integration
screens.narratorSegment: A Pull Request is a formal proposal to merge one branch into another. It is both a technical operation and a social one: opening a PR asks teammates to review changes, discuss design decisions, and verify tests. PRs give a place for inline comments, change requests, and approval, which improves code quality and shared understanding. The typical PR workflow starts with creating a feature branch, making commits there, pushing the branch to the remote, and then opening a PR targeting main. Reviewers examine the diff, comment, and request changes. The author addresses feedback, updates the branch, and pushes additional commits; the PR automatically updates. Once approved, the reviewer or an automated policy merges the branch into main. A common misconception is that a PR is only for permission; instead, treat it as a lightweight design review. Tools like required reviews and CI checks can block merges until tests pass. Concrete example: after pushing feature/add-calculator, open a PR, ask for at least one reviewer, and include a description explaining why the change is safe. Final question: how does the PR record help future team members understand why a change was made? The PR discussion and commit history provide context that a single commit message cannot.

narration.text: A Pull Request is a formal proposal to merge one branch into another. It is both a technical operation and a social one: opening a PR asks teammates to review changes, discuss design decisions, and verify tests. PRs give a place for inline comments, change requests, and approval, which improves code quality and shared understanding. The typical PR workflow starts with creating a feature branch, making commits there, pushing the branch to the remote, and then opening a PR targeting main. Reviewers examine the diff, comment, and request changes. The author addresses feedback, updates the branch, and pushes additional commits; the PR automatically updates. Once approved, the reviewer or an automated policy merges the branch into main. A common misconception is that a PR is only for permission; instead, treat it as a lightweight design review. Tools like required reviews and CI checks can block merges until tests pass. Concrete example: after pushing feature/add-calculator, open a PR, ask for at least one reviewer, and include a description explaining why the change is safe. Final question: how does the PR record help future team members understand why a change was made? The PR discussion and commit history provide context that a single commit message cannot.

keyIdea.title: PR purpose
keyIdea.text: Pull Requests create a reviewable snapshot of changes and a shared space for discussion, tests, and approval before merging.

content.html:
Core Concept
Pull Requests
Open a PR to request review, run CI, and discuss the change before merging into main.
Typical PR Workflow
  1. Create and push a feature branch.
  2. Open a Pull Request targeting main with a clear description.
  3. Reviewers comment and request changes if needed.
  4. Author updates the branch and pushes additional commits.
  5. When approved and CI passes, merge the PR and delete the branch if desired.
Concrete Example
Push feature/add-calculator and open a PR. In the PR description explain the change and list any manual testing steps so reviewers can validate behavior quickly.
Misconception
A Pull Request is not just a gatekeeper. Use it to transfer knowledge, explain trade-offs, and document decisions for future readers.

screens.title: GitHub Flow vs Git Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Branching strategies define how teams name branches, where they merge, and how releases are managed. GitHub Flow is simple and great for teams that deploy frequently: main is always deployable, and all work happens on short-lived feature branches that are merged into main via Pull Requests. This keeps the workflow light and fast. Git Flow is more structured and often used for projects with formal release cycles. It introduces long-lived branches such as develop, release, and hotfix alongside main. Developers merge feature branches into develop; releases come from release branches and hotfixes fix production issues directly into main and develop. A common misconception is that Git Flow is necessarily better; in practice, choose the strategy that suits your release cadence. For most small projects and early-stage teams, GitHub Flow’s simplicity is an advantage. For complex release planning, Git Flow can help coordinate multiple release lines. Concrete decision: if your team deploys daily and values fast iteration, prefer GitHub Flow. If your product requires staged releases and versioned maintenance, consider Git Flow. Takeaway: pick a convention, document it, and make sure everyone follows the same rules to avoid confusion.

keyIdea.text: GitHub Flow for fast continuous deployment; Git Flow for structured release management. Consistency matters more than which you pick.

content.html:
Comparison
GitHub Flow
Main is always deployable; feature branches are short-lived and merged via PRs.
Pros: simple, fast, fits continuous deployment.
Cons: less structure for complex release planning.
Git Flow
Uses develop, release, and hotfix branches alongside main to coordinate versioned releases.
Pros: clear release stages and long-term maintenance lines.
Cons: more overhead and merge complexity for frequent deploys.
Key Takeaway

Choose the strategy to match your release cadence, then standardize naming and merge practices across the team.

screens.title: Keep Feature Branches Up-to-Date
screens.narratorSegment: A practical habit to avoid painful merges is keeping your feature branches up-to-date with main. Regularly pull the latest main into your feature branch or rebase selectively to minimize divergence. If you use merge: switch to your feature branch and run git pull origin main or git merge origin/main after fetching. If you prefer rebase, run git fetch origin and git rebase origin/main on your feature branch, remembering that rebasing rewrites history and should be used carefully on public branches. The important point is not which technique you pick but that you integrate main frequently so your local changes remain compatible. This reduces the size and complexity of eventual merges and makes conflicts easier to resolve because they appear incrementally. A common mistake is postponing syncs until release time, which multiplies conflicts into a large, error-prone session. For teams, document whether rebasing is allowed and require short-lived branches. Concrete habit: at the start of each day or before opening a PR, sync your branch with the latest main to surface conflicts early. Final takeaway: frequent, small integrations beat infrequent large ones.

keyIdea.title: Integrate often
keyIdea.text: Sync your feature branch with main frequently to discover conflicts early and keep merges manageable.

content.html:
Best Practice
Keep Branches Up-to-Date
Integrate main into your branch regularly to reduce the size and difficulty of merges.
Merge approach
git fetch origin
git switch feature/add-calculator
git merge origin/main
Rebase approach (use with care)
git fetch origin
git switch feature/add-calculator
git rebase origin/main
Rebasing rewrites commit history. Avoid rebasing public branches shared with collaborators unless everyone agrees to the workflow.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Tips for Smooth Collaboration
screens.narratorSegment: Collaboration problems often stem from small process issues. Here are common mistakes and tips to avoid them. First, long-lived branches tend to drift; prefer short-lived feature branches and integrate frequently. Second, forgetting to stage resolved files after conflict resolution prevents the merge commit—always run git add on resolved files. Third, unclear commit messages or branch names make reviews harder; use descriptive branch names and conventional commit messages like feat: or fix:. Fourth, not running tests locally before pushing causes flaky CI; run your test suite locally and address failures before opening a Pull Request. Fifth, deleting merged branches keeps the remote tidy. For each tip, pair it with a practice: push often, rebase or merge main regularly, and run tests before a PR. A practical pro-tip: include a short description and testing steps in each Pull Request to speed up review. The misconception to avoid is treating GitHub as only a backup; it is the team’s collaboration surface. Final reflection: which habit could you add this week to reduce conflicts and speed reviews? Common Mistakes and Tips for Smooth Collaboration means short branches, good names, local tests, and staging resolved files prevent common problems and speed integration.. In practical terms, practical checklist to avoid errors and keep the repo healthy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Mistake
Long-lived branches that drift from main make merges painful. Keep features small and merge often.
Mistake
Forgetting git add after resolving conflicts prevents the merge commit—stage resolved files before committing.
Tip
Use clear branch names and commit messages. Include testing steps in PR descriptions to accelerate review.
Try This
Before opening your next Pull Request, run your tests, sync with main, and add a concise PR checklist: what you changed, why, and how to validate it.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: As you finish this lesson, keep three core concepts front of mind. First, GitHub and similar remotes host shared history and provide Pull Requests and Issues that turn commits into collaborative, reviewable work. Second, branching isolates development so teams can iterate in parallel: create short-lived, descriptive branches, commit often, and keep them synced with main. Third, merge conflicts are a normal part of collaboration—you resolve them by editing conflict markers, staging the resolved files, and committing. Each idea supports the central goal: keep main deployable while enabling parallel work and review. If you adopt consistent naming, clear commit messages, and the habit of syncing branches often, you reduce friction and make code review faster. Remember that PRs are social tools as much as technical ones; use them to explain, request feedback, and document decisions for future readers. With these practices, merge conflicts become manageable moments for team coordination rather than blockers to progress.

keyIdea.title: Remember

GitHub / Remote
A remote hosts your repo and provides Issues and Pull Requests for team collaboration and CI integration.
Branching

You will learn how platforms like GitHub host your repository online so teammates can push, pull, review, and merge code. More than file storage, GitHub gives you Issues, Pull Requests, and a visible history that supports collaboration and review for quality. We’ll also unpack branching: why you create isolated branches for features or fixes, how to switch and commit on those branches, and how merging brings changes back into a stable main branch. You will see a concrete scenario where a feature branch and main both change the same file, produce a merge conflict, and how to resolve it safely. Finally, we’ll compare simple GitHub Flow and the more structured Git Flow so you can choose a branching strategy that fits your project. By the end, you’ll understand the social and technical steps—create branch, commit, push, open a Pull Request, review, merge—so your team can evolve code confidently. Consider how this workflow preserves a deployable main branch while enabling many parallel contributors.

In this module you will build practical skills for collaborative Git workflows. First, you will explain the role of GitHub and similar hosting platforms: what happens when you push or pull, and why a remote repository matters for team visibility. Second, you will understand branching as an isolated line of development and when to choose a new branch for a feature or a hotfix. Third, you will create, switch between, and merge branches using real commands, and practice committing and pushing your changes so others can review them. Fourth, you will identify and resolve merge conflicts that occur when two branches change the same lines, and demonstrate the correct staging and commit steps to finalize a merge. Each objective emphasizes both the commands and the reasoning behind them, so you can apply the workflow on your team. We'll use concrete examples like adding a Calculator class and simulating conflicting edits to HelloWorld. java to practice these skills. By the end, you'll confidently open a Pull Request, respond to review feedback, and integrate changes while keeping main deployable.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied practice. You will learn the precise sequence of commands used in a typical feature workflow: create a branch, make commits, push the branch to the remote, open a Pull Request, handle requested changes, and merge. We reinforce the correct conflict workflow: when Git stops a merge, inspect the conflict markers, edit to decide what to keep, stage the resolved files with git add, then commit to finish the merge. You will practice both the safe habit of keeping main deployable and the practical habit of pulling main into long-lived feature branches frequently to reduce conflict complexity. We’ll also show how GitHub Flow emphasizes short-lived branches and fast merges, while Git Flow uses develop, release, and hotfix branches for controlled release processes. Each objective pairs a command sequence with a short hands-on task: add Calculator. java on a feature branch, make a conflicting HelloWorld. java change on main, then merge and resolve the conflict. These repeated steps build muscle memory so you avoid common mistakes like forgetting to stage resolved files before committing.

A remote repository is the shared copy of your project that lives on a hosting service such as GitHub. The remote stores commits pushed by contributors and acts as the authoritative source for collaboration. When you run git push, your local commits are uploaded to the remote so teammates can fetch or pull them into their local clones. Conversely, git pull fetches and merges remote commits into your current branch. GitHub adds social and workflow tools on top of this: Issues to track bugs and requests, Pull Requests for proposing code integration, and a web-based diff viewer for reviews. This combination is powerful: it separates local experimentation from shared history and creates a visible record that supports review, discussion, and CI automation. For a concrete example, if one teammate pushes a feature branch called feature/add-calculator, others can open that branch on GitHub, comment on specific lines, and run tests against it before merging. A common misconception is thinking the remote replaces local history; instead, it complements local repositories by providing a central place to coordinate and recover work. Key takeaway: push and pull are the networked actions that connect local branches to the team’s shared workflow, enabling review and integration without forcing everyone to share a single working copy.

Branching creates an independent line of development that lets you work on a feature or fix without affecting the stable main branch. Conceptually, each branch is a pointer into the commit history; commits made on that branch form a separate timeline. Choose branch names that communicate purpose, for example feature/add-calculator or fix/typo-hello. Good names make code review and repository navigation easier for teammates. The default branch is usually main. When you initialize a repository, you start on main and then create short-lived branches for work. This isolation is crucial: if your feature fails tests or introduces bugs, main remains deployable. A common mistake is doing large, long-lived work on a branch without regularly syncing with main. That increases the chance of complex conflicts later. Instead, keep branches small and integrate often. For a concrete example, create feature/add-calculator and implement Calculator. java with an add method, commit, and push. This keeps the new code separate until reviewers approve it. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Practically creating and switching branches is how you start isolated work. The commands are straightforward: git branch creates a branch, git switch or git checkout changes your working branch, and git checkout -b or git switch -c creates and switches in a single step. In this walkthrough you’ll enact a realistic sequence: start on main, create feature/add-calculator, add Calculator. java, stage and commit, then push the branch to the remote. Merging brings changes from one branch into another. There are two common merge outcomes. If the target branch has no new commits since the feature branched, Git can perform a fast-forward merge by simply moving the target pointer forward to include the feature commits. A merge conflict happens when Git cannot reconcile two changes to the same part of a file. Your task is to open the file, review both versions, decide which lines to keep or how to combine them, and then remove all markers. A common mistake is to resolve the textual conflict but forget to git add the file; Git will continue to wait for the staged resolution and you cannot complete the merge. Another pitfall is to accept one side blindly when a combined or reconciled version is better. Use your editor or IDE merge tools where possible, and run your tests after resolving. For a concrete walkthrough, we’ll use HelloWorld. java, which gets different console lines on main and on the feature branch. Resolve by keeping both lines or choosing the best phrasing, then stage and commit. The closing insight: conflicts are normal—treat them as a deliberate code-review moment and communicate with your teammate if unsure.
